scope_note: Support, uptime SLA, backups and money-back guarantee for 21 hosting providers. Every figure was read on 2026-08-18 from a provider-operated URL and is recorded with that URL. Where a figure sits behind a login, a configurator, a quote form or a document that would not render, the field is null and the reason is stated in a note.
method_note: Three reading methods were used and are distinguished in the notes where it matters: direct page fetch, server-side HTML extraction for pages whose text is server-rendered, and a headless browser for pages that render their content in JavaScript. No figure in this file comes from a third-party comparison site, a search snippet alone, or memory. Where a search engine surfaced a claim that could not be confirmed on the provider's own page, the claim was dropped rather than recorded.
vocabulary_note: A contractual SLA is a published document that states an availability percentage, a remedy, and a claim procedure. A marketing uptime claim is a percentage printed on a product or pricing page with no remedy attached. The two are recorded in separate fields and are not merged.
remedy_note: Every SLA in this file that has a remedy pays it in service credits against future invoices. Not one of the 21 pays money back for downtime. Several state expressly that credits have no cash value. This is the norm, not an outlier, and it is recorded per provider rather than editorialised.
price_note: All prices carry the capture date 2026-08-18, a currency, and the URL they were read from. Support-plan prices are list prices, not introductory offers, so is_promotional is false on each of them. Where a provider quotes both a fixed fee and a percentage of spend, both are recorded along with which one applies.

cross_provider_observations: Genuinely 24/7 human technical support at no extra cost, on the pages read: IONOS (the Cloud SLA states 24/7/365 support at no additional charge with a sub-1-hour disruption response), DigitalOcean (ticket access 24/7 on the free Starter plan, though the target is under 24 hours), Scaleway (BASIC ticketing 24/7 with an 8-hour target), WP Engine (24/7 chat on every plan, phone from the Professional plan up), Kinsta (24/7/365 chat included in all plan levels), SiteGround and Hostinger (24/7 marketed on hosting pages), Hetzner (24/7 by email for Cloud, with 24/7 phone limited to the data centre lines) and Akamai (phone described as available day and night, no tiers).

Support is paywalled, and the price is the interesting part: AWS from USD 29 per month or 9% of charges (whichever is greater) for Business Support+, rising to a USD 5,000 per month floor for Enterprise and USD 50,000 for Unified Operations; Google Cloud USD 29 for Standard, USD 100 minimum plus 10-3% tiers for Enhanced, USD 15,000 minimum for Premium; Azure USD 29 Developer, USD 100 Standard, USD 1,000 Professional Direct; OVHcloud EUR 50 Premium, then 10% of the bill with a EUR 250 floor for 24/7 Business and 30% with a EUR 5,000 floor for Enterprise; Scaleway EUR 50/5%, EUR 250/10%, EUR 990/20%; Exoscale EUR 50, EUR 500, then 5% of usage with a EUR 1,500 floor for 24/7; Infomaniak EUR 50, EUR 250 and EUR 1,000 (or 10% of monthly product value) on a six-month minimum; DigitalOcean USD 24, USD 99, USD 999; Fly.io USD 29, USD 199, from USD 2,500.

Percentage-of-spend pricing is the pattern to watch. AWS, Google Cloud, OVHcloud, Scaleway, Exoscale and Infomaniak all bill support as the greater of a floor or a percentage of the bill, and Google states the percentage is calculated on list prices before any discounts or credits. Support cost therefore scales with infrastructure spend and a negotiated infrastructure discount does not reduce it.

The three hyperscalers' free tier is billing support. AWS Basic, Azure Basic and Google Cloud Basic all provide account and billing help, documentation and dashboards, and none provides a technical support case with an engineer or a response-time target.

Marketing uptime claims without a matching contractual remedy, on the pages read: SiteGround advertises 99.99% on cloud hosting pages while its Terms of Service guarantee a single figure of 99.9% with a 5% compensation that can only extend the service term; IONOS titles its web hosting page 99.99% Uptime while the contractual IONOS Cloud compute commitment is 99.95% and Cloud GPU VM is excluded from the SLA entirely; Infomaniak advertises 99.99% on product pages and no published SLA document with a percentage, remedy and claim procedure was located.

Availability commitments that exist only above the paywall: Vercel 99.99% for Enterprise only, with Hobby and Pro carrying no commitment; Netlify 99.99% for Enterprise only, with the remedy living in an unpublished Order Form; Fly.io 99.9% for Enterprise plan customers, from USD 2,500 per month; Render and Railway publish no availability percentage at all for self-serve plans and offer an SLA only under a negotiated Enterprise contract.

Two providers publish an SLA whose scope excludes what a reader would assume it covers. Vultr guarantees 100% uptime but excludes its own web property, DNS servers, API and control panel, excludes GPU instances entirely, and starts the outage clock at the timestamp of a ticket that must itself request a credit. Vercel's SLA excludes components that do not serve customer content, naming the API and CLI.

The single-instance versus multi-zone gap runs through all three hyperscalers. AWS commits 99.99% only across two or more Availability Zones and 99.5% for one instance; Google commits 99.99% for instances in multiple zones and 99.9% for a single instance of a standard family; Azure commits 99.99% only across two or more Availability Zones, 99.95% in an availability set and 99.9% for a single VM with premium SSDs. The headline number requires an architecture the headline price does not include.

Scaleway is the outlier on the downside: covered shared instances commit to 99%, covered dedicated and GPU instances to 99.5%, and the DEV1, GP1, PLAY2, PRO2, COPARM1, ENT1 and DEV instance types have no service level objective at all.

Every remedy in this file is a credit, never money. Hetzner, Scaleway, OVHcloud, IONOS, Exoscale, DigitalOcean, Vultr, Akamai, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, WP Engine, Kinsta, SiteGround, Hostinger, Vercel and Fly.io all pay in credits against future invoices, and several state expressly that credits have no cash value and expire. DigitalOcean credits expire after 90 days; Vultr credits expire after one year; Kinsta and WP Engine credits are forfeited on termination.

The claim is on the customer, and the windows are short. Hetzner 14 days after month end, IONOS two weeks after the billing month, Vultr three days from the triggering event, Fly.io 30 days after month end and only if the outage was reported when it happened, Kinsta 30 days via chat, WP Engine 30 days, Scaleway 30 days with log files, Vercel 30 days with log files, Akamai 30 days, AWS by the end of the second billing cycle, DigitalOcean within two billing cycles, OVHcloud US 60 days. No provider in this set pays credits automatically without a claim.

Backups are an extra almost everywhere in the VPS and cloud category and included almost everywhere in the managed WordPress and shared category. Extra: Hetzner 20% of the server price, DigitalOcean 20% weekly or 30% daily (or per-GiB rates from USD 0.01 to USD 0.04), Vultr 20% of the instance price, Akamai from USD 2 per month per plan, OVHcloud a paid VPS option, Exoscale snapshots billed per GiB.hour on the source volume size, and the hyperscalers metering snapshots and backup services separately. Included: WP Engine daily with 30 days retention, Kinsta daily with 14 to 30 days by tier, SiteGround daily with restore points up to 30 days, IONOS daily with data recovery, Hostinger weekly with two weeks stored.

Snapshots are billed as storage almost universally, which means the backup line on the invoice grows with the disk rather than staying with the plan: Hetzner per GB per month, Vultr USD 0.05 per GB per month on the compressed size, DigitalOcean per GiB of restorable size on usage-based plans, Exoscale per GiB.hour of the source volume size, and all three hyperscalers per GB-month.

Backup coverage gaps that a comparison tick would hide: Hetzner backups and snapshots exclude attached Volumes, Vultr backups exclude attached block storage, Akamai backups exclude attached Volumes and are deleted with the instance, OVHcloud's VPS backup service excludes additional disks, and Hostinger removes any cPanel shared account over 30 GB from the offsite weekly backup.

Money-back guarantees exist in the managed and shared category and essentially nowhere else. Kinsta 30 days for first-time customers, excluding dedicated server fees, one-time fees and overages; SiteGround 30 days shared and 14 days cloud, excluding domains and paid support; Hostinger 30 days, excluding crypto payments, with a 180-day cooldown after a VPS refund; IONOS 30 days. Against that: DigitalOcean states all fees are non-refundable, Vultr states it does not guarantee refunds, and no money-back guarantee was found for Hetzner, OVHcloud, Scaleway, Exoscale, Akamai, AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, WP Engine, Vercel, Netlify, Fly.io or Render.
